cards.b:
Feminists say traditional theories ignored one huge fact: the state has mostly been run by men, and it has protected patriarchy, the system of male dominance.

Their key slogan was "the personal is political", popularised by Carol Hanisch's 1970 essay. Even what happens inside the home is shaped by power and law.

Liberal feminists see the state as basically neutral but biased in practice. The answer is reform: equal rights, equal pay, voting rights and anti-discrimination laws.

Thinkers include Mary Wollstonecraft (A Vindication of the Rights of Woman, 1792), J.S. Mill (The Subjection of Women, 1869) and Betty Friedan (The Feminine Mystique, 1963).

Radical feminists say patriarchy is built into the state itself. Reform is not enough.

"The state is male in the feminist sense: the law sees and treats women the way men see and treat women."
Catharine MacKinnon, Toward a Feminist Theory of the State (1989)

Kate Millett's Sexual Politics (1970) is another key text.

In The Sexual Contract (1988), Pateman argued that the famous social contract of Hobbes and Locke hides an earlier sexual contract.

Men agreed among themselves on access to women's bodies and labour. Women were never parties to the contract, only its subjects. So the liberal state was patriarchal from the start.

Socialist and Marxist feminists link patriarchy to capitalism. Women's unpaid domestic work reproduces the workforce for free, which benefits capital.

The state supports both systems together. Thinkers include Juliet Mitchell and Heidi Hartmann, who called the link an "unhappy marriage" of Marxism and feminism.

• Intersectionality. Kimberlé Crenshaw (1989) showed that race, class and gender overlap. White middle-class feminism ignored many women.
  • Post-colonial feminism. Chandra Talpade Mohanty's "Under Western Eyes" (1984) criticised Western feminists for treating "Third World women" as one helpless group.
  • State as ally? The state has also passed laws protecting women, so it is not only an oppressor.

Later feminists asked: which women does feminism speak for?

Chandra Talpade Mohanty

In "Under Western Eyes" (1984/1986), she criticised Western feminists for treating "Third World women" as one passive, oppressed victim group.

Gayatri Chakravorty Spivak

In "Can the Subaltern Speak?" (1988), she used the British ban on sati to show how both colonisers and local elites spoke for subaltern women, never letting them speak.

bell hooks

In Ain't I a Woman (1981), she showed how racism and sexism combine for Black women.

These ideas feed into intersectionality: the state treats a poor Dalit woman differently from a rich upper-caste woman, so gender alone cannot explain her position.

The Indian state has a mixed record. It brought the 73rd and 74th Amendments (1992), reserving a third of local body seats for women. The 106th Amendment (2023), known as Nari Shakti Vandan Adhiniyam, reserves a third of Lok Sabha and state assembly seats for women, effective after the next census and delimitation.

But Dalit feminists like Sharmila Rege show how caste and gender combine, which links to Ambedkar's view that caste is maintained by controlling women.

"The state is male." Discuss with reference to feminist theory.

Structure: quote MacKinnon, then cover the three strands (liberal, radical, socialist). Add Pateman's sexual contract and intersectionality. End with India's reservation laws as evidence that the state can be both a site of oppression and of change.
